lesson.title: Cuenta y Lanza: A Ten-Frame Beanbag Toss
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: Sol found a ten-frame today — ten little boxes in two rows! Grab some beanbags (or rolled-up socks), because we're going to toss and count all the way to ten.
Sol holds up a card with a number on it and says [[el número]] — that means 'number'! Every number you toss and count today — seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez — is a número Sol wants to hear.
Now it's your turn: toss a beanbag into a box of the ten-frame, counting out loud from uno all the way up. Keep tossing until every box has one and you've said diez!
You counted every beanbag toss out loud, from uno all the way to diez, saying every número along the way! Tomorrow, we'll go hunting for hidden number cards.

config.instructions: Match the Spanish number to how many it means.

objectives: Count aloud from uno to diez while tossing beanbags into a ten-frame, one toss per box
materialsNeeded: A simple ten-frame drawn on paper or chalk (two rows of five boxes)
A few soft beanbags, rolled-up socks, or scrunched paper balls
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Draw or set up a ten-frame — two rows of five boxes — on the floor or a table.
2. Have Sol hold up a card with a number on it and explain that número means 'number' in Spanish.
3. Take turns tossing a beanbag toward the ten-frame, counting the running total out loud together each time: uno, dos, tres...
4. Keep tossing until you reach diez, filling every box in the ten-frame.
5. Ask your child which número was hardest to say, then try a second round tossing in a different order.
6. Complete the on-screen matching activity together, reading each number aloud since your child may not read yet.
7. Close by asking: 'What word means number in Spanish?'
differentiationTips: Struggling: stop counting at ocho for the first round and add nueve, diez once the sequence feels steady
Ready for more: have your child count silently while tossing, then announce only the final número once the ten-frame is full
A beanbag that misses the ten-frame still gets counted — the goal is confident counting, not accuracy of the toss
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is a spoken counting-and-tossing activity — success looks like your child counting tosses aloud from uno toward diez, not a written answer. In the matching game: seis → 6️⃣, siete → 7️⃣, ocho → 8️⃣, nueve → 9️⃣, diez → 🔟, el número → 🔢 number.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Continues week 4's WA-WL-2015.1.3 target by having the child produce the running count out loud during a physical toss rather than just echo it, and introduces número as the word for the very thing being counted — giving this week's numbers a name of their own, the way contar named week 3's counting action.
